utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, yesterday my fellow Judges here, Judge Stephen and Judge Vohrah, explained to me what you were trying to explain to me yesterday evening, and that is that you would prefer not to have a witness who would begin his or her testimony and then that testimony be interrupted and not be concluded considering the two week recess that we are going to have. That is what you were asking me. I apologise for not understanding better. I did not hear it that way. So, the answer is that we agree that should be avoided because there, I gather, would be a need to put up a witness, to provide for lodging etc. over this period of time, or incur the expense of sending the witness back to wherever the witness is from. That is not the best procedure. So let us see how we proceed today and it might not happen, but if it appears that we are going to get to a point where you would call a witness and we would not complete the witness, then you will simply not call that witness. Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's next witness is Kemal Susic. ^^ MR. KEMAL SUSIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you take the oath that is being given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also ask you to have it a bit louder because I can barely hear.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you turn up the volume? Will you turn up the volume, please? Can you hear me now, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is slightly better.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, now is all right. Now it is all right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Sir, your name is Kemal Susic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Kozarac, on 20th October 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you live there your entire life until the outbreak of the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On what street in Kozarac did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived on the street of Marsala Tita bb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that in central Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may have this photograph marked next in order for identification which, I believe, is 241? Mr. Susic, do you recognise what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to explain -----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you quickly if that shows the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and this is my town Kozarac before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am going to ask to have that exhibit tendered for admission and if there is no objection and if it is admitted, I would like it called up as Z5-31 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 241 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, can the home in which you lived be seen in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is this one, the biggest building. I lived on the second floor of that building to the left facing Mountain Kozara. That is the second floor. It was a four storey building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, are you referring to the multi-storey building which appears slightly to the right of centre in the photograph? You can see the small arrow, does that -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this mark here and it is indicating that particular building in which I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you also see any of the mosques of Kozarac in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment I see three mosques here, Mutnik Mosque, a mosque in the very heart of Kozarac, and I can see the mosque in Brdjani and I see also the mosque in Stari Grad, in the old town, also in the heart of Kozarac. So I see three mosques here. I think that this photograph was taken from the minaret of another mosque which is in Kalate. That is what this looks like, the vista, that is before me, I think, could be from the minaret of that mosque which I believe was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, I am going ask to have the photograph placed on this machine to your right so can you quickly point out these mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please focus it? Thank you. Now it is all right. This mosque here is ---

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- Mutnik Mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you could point to the actual photograph, we will be able to see where you are pointing. Then you can use the pointer, if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Mutnik Mosque. This is Stari Grad mosque, old town mosque. This is the mosque in Brdjani, this one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So going from left to right in the photograph, on the left side we see the Mutnik Mosque in the middle and ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- up toward the top we see Brdjani mosque and toward the right we see the Stari Grad mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to the right. Yes, you are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may, I would like to show you a very brief portion of a video. I would like you to tell me if you can find your home on that video. So if we could show that small portion of Exhibit 195, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us to stop when you see your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop, please. This is the building I lived in. This is a four storeyed building, and a few months before the war a supermarket was opened there, but the entrance is from the other side. On this shot I can see that the flats had been put on fire. What happened on the other side, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I add something more?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I mean, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, that is fine, sir. Thank you. Sir, did your family live in Kozarac for some generations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We have seen some photographs of the police station on Marsala Tita. Do you know what that building was or who it belonged to before it was the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The building belonged to my grandfather, that is, my mother's father, and after World War II it was confiscated through nationalisation and not only that building but several more buildings in Kozarac. When we were children we lived in that building, and on one occasion the then Mayor of the municipality, Bozo Dragicevic, a man of Serb origin, came to our house and said we had to leave the house because it would become a school. At that time in Kozarac there were also other buildings which could serve the purposes of a school. However, the events then evidently meant that we had to leave the house that we lived in and we took it very hard. At that time my mother's father was still alive, but that old man in a very advanced age could not do anything. He was simply helpless. Should I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, that is fine, thank you. Mr. Susic, what was your occupation before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked the primary school Rade Kondic in Kozarac. I am an educator. I teach physical education.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long did you teach physical education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I began to work for the primary school in Kozarac in '68, in August, until practically the outbreak of the war, practically to the last day I was with my pupils. The problems that preceded the war and then the war circumstances took us gradually out of the school rooms, both the teachers and pupils. It was not possible any more to conduct any instruction. It was really very hard to describe. We were all very worried, both children and teachers. We spent more days talking and discussing than working.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will get to those segments of the conflict. Let me ask first, however, if you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic's family, that is, his father Ostoja Tadic, is in the very heart of Kozarac, and from my father's house it is at some 100 to 200 metres away from my father's house. So, Dusko, his mother, his father, lived in Kozarac and we knew each other very well. Dusko Tadic was also a pupil of mine. When I came to work there I believe he was in the fifth grade of the primary school. At that time how I remember Dusko, Dusko was a very nice boy, like all the other children. He was not distinguishable from others. He grew up normally. We lived normally, and we befriended each other. We socialised, regardless whether those children were of Serb or of Muslim origin. I also know Dusko's brothers, Mladen, Ljubomir, and Stojan. Stojan was a school fellow of mine and I know him very well. I also know his mother, Staka. She is a very fine woman. Dusko Tadic's father in World War II fought in World War II. He fought from the beginning of the war. He was a war veteran and a man who joined the fighting in the early days of the war and after the war he had a good -- he thus earned a good pension after the war. So they were never bad off. They lived there. They lived nicely. Should I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, that is fine. Did you know Dusko Tadic's wife and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did know his wife and she was also a pupil of mine. I would not be able to say whether for a year or two, but she was my pupil. His elder daughter I also know in the fifth grade. She was my pupil too. His younger daughter, I do not because she simply was not in one of the grades I taught. She was too young for that. Dusko's wife's name is Mira.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated you were a physical education professor. Did Dusko Tadic use the gym at your school to train young people in karate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, in Kozarac that gym was the only gym. There were quite a number of people interested in using that gym because we have different sections, a school, then the Fire Brigade that we had, the football club in Kozarac. It was very difficult to get time there, and Dusko himself knows that I was one of the people who helped him get access to that hall, to that gym, so as to coach our children, children of Kozarac, in marshal arts. I thought it was natural and normal and that was all right because they were all our children and Dusko was one of our children, and I never thought, I could never think about any problems or any difficulties that might arise which would not allow Dusko to use that gym. As far as I know, the school asked for no compensation, for no fee. Dusko Tadic did not have to pay anything for the use of the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When Dusko Tadic built his cafe, did any members of your family help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic's family, as far as I know, his brother Ljubomir and Dusko were building the house and the coffee bar together. The coffee bar was added slightly later. First, the house was completed and a large number of young people in Kozarac, especially those who were coached in karate by Dusko, neighbours and friends, came to work there and help to build Dusko's house and Dusko's cafe. As far as I know, those people asked for no remuneration and even my younger son went to help, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did any member of your family loan money to Dusko Tadic to help finance the building of the cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Kozarac I had an uncle, a man who was well off, who was a wealthy man, and Dusko borrowed from him a certain sum, a certain amount of money, so as to complete his coffee bar. I could not tell you the exact amount of money that was borrowed. All I do know is that there were not any particular problems regarding the returning of that money. Whether Dusko returned all this money to this uncle of mine, I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the years in which you knew Mr. Tadic, I take it you became quite familiar with his appearance. Can you describe quickly his general build during the time you knew him, his physique?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As an athlete, a sportsman, Dusko Tadic is well built, athletic build, strong muscles. He is of a medium height, and he walks -- he has a very firm step.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the years you knew him did he sometimes have a beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes he did, sometimes he did not, so, so. I guess it depended on the mood. Sometimes he had a beard and he shaved it off and so. That was a natural phenomenon everywhere and with us too a fad, perhaps. He was not often with a beard. After all, it was his own free choice, his free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you ever see or hear of anyone in the Kozarac area or opstina Prijedor generally who looked enough like Dusko Tadic that he was mistaken for Dusko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could miss -- that I could be wrong about it, I think it would be very difficult because I have known Dusko Tadic almost since the day he was born. They grew up almost before my eyes. They used the same street that I used. I could recognise that man even at a bigger distance, even in the darkness perhaps, and even if he were turn -- he had his back turned on me, I could always recognise him because he has a rather characteristic gait and his build is also rather characteristic. He also speaks in a rather characteristic manner. I do not really see that I could easily mistake some other man for Dusko Tadic. I am quite positive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, let me ask you what relations were like between Serbs and Muslims in the time you were growing up and up to the time preceding the conflict, just in general, were they good or bad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me point out straightaway that relations were good, and to go back in time a little, while I was a little younger, in our homes, as far as I know at least, in the homes of Muslims and especially in my home and the home of my father, we never said of somebody that he was of Serb ethnicity or Croat ethnicity or anything else. We played together. We grew up together. We went to school together and we were very good friends. I was a very good friend with his brother Stojan, for instance. We were of the same age, the same generation. Dusko is younger. Ljubomir is younger, so is Mladen. I was also a good friend and grew up with Simo Miskovic, I and my brothers and the other children of Kozarac. Simo Miskovic would come often to visit my home and when he grew up, got married and moved to Prijedor, he would talk about the wonderful days he had in Kozarac as a boy which he could not forget. We would play together. Afterwards we would go to my mother's who would serve food for all of us, give us fruit, regardless of what ethnic group we belonged to. We felt free, we grew up normally. Simo Miskovic's brother Ranko was also there. That man has died. On one occasion -- no, let me not tire you with the details because one could write a novel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You said that people did not distinguish between Muslims and Serbs. Was it possible to distinguish between a Serb and a Muslim based on the way that person looked physically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I think it is very difficult to say. After all, we are all the same. Only the people in the villages, on the slopes of Kozara, differed in so much that the Muslim women differed from the Serb women, because they wore typical costumes, a long skirt and black scarves. This was worn by Serb women. So this could be noticed. We spoke the same language. The Ijekavac dialect and not the Ekavac dialect, which is characteristic of the Republic of Serbia. But my colleague who worked with me at school, Milos Radulovic, though he had spent some 30 years in Bosnia, never changed his dialect, the Ekavac for Ijekavac. He worked with children in the school yet he still spoke the Ekavac dialect. Sometimes I would make a joke as we were good colleagues, I said, "How come you have not accepted our way of speech?" He would say, "I just speak like that. I come from Serbia". This did not bother anybody. These were our normal conversations. But people born in Kozarac coming from these parts all spoke the Ijekavac dialect. There were no differences between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could you tell who was a Serb and a Muslim sometimes based on that person's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, the names of Muslims and Serbs differ. They are typical names, so that in that respect or by that we knew whether someone was a Muslim or a Serb by their names. If somebody is called "Muhamed", then he is a Muslim, we know that. But if is somebody is called "Miko", "Ranko" or "Jovan", then we know that he is a Serb; only by that could we tell, in no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the period of time between the elections in 1990 and the outbreak of the conflict in 1992, was there the beginning of a change in the relations between the ethnic groups and the beginning of tension?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me see. Marked tension began to be noticed immediately prior to the aggression against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina because some towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina had already experienced on their own hide, they had personal experience of the growing Serb nationalism, linked with the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Susic, I wanted to focus you a little closer to Kozarac at the moment, and ask you if you saw some signs of growing tension in your own school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we are talking about my school in particular, the school I worked in, as I had a specific post, I had my own office next to the gymnasium for physical education, going to the teachers' room I could see that gradually groups began to be formed, on the one side teachers of Muslim ethnicity, on the other teachers of Serb ethnicity. I knew what that meant, and it bothered me a little. There was nothing I could do. What is more, I did not know what they were talking about, but it was already clear to me as soon as I saw that they were separate that something was not in order, that something was wrong. One of the colleagues working with me of Serb ethnicity, a teacher of general technical education, Milos Radulovic, said on one occasion that he, as a Serb in Kozarac, was in jeopardy. I did not like that. I wanted to ask him what was wrong. I asked him to come to my office for us to have a chat and I asked, "What is the problem?" He simply could not give me a specific answer why he felt endangered as a Serb in Kozarac. I told him, "Mico, you are probably in jeopardy because you came to Kozarac with a wooden suitcase, and then the Rade Kondic school provided a studio for you, after that a two-room apartment, after that you built yourself a beautiful house, and probably that is why you are in jeopardy, because many of the people of Kozarac came to your aid to help you build your house". People would bring him sand, building material, timber, for free. He and others like him who spread alleged fears were simply looking for reasons for a separation. They wanted differences in views and positions to surface and gradually that rift became deeper and gradually we moved away more and more, one from another. That is as much as I could say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Shortly before the attack on Kozarac, did you become involved in a group that was attempting to resolve issues peacefully, become involved in a peace group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Sarajevo was attacked, we saw that something terrible was about to happen in Bosnia. At that time the Party of Democratic Action in Prijedor at the regular elections won and came into power in Prijedor. However, the events that preceded this led to a gap being formed, the already formed Serbian Democratic Party on the one hand and the Muslim party, the SDA. Any dialogue or normal human conversation or a joint meeting between representatives of those parties could hardly be organised. That is why several of us people from Kozarac, on our own initiative, met and talked and set up a group which we freely decided to call the League for Peace. We thought, since we did not belong to any Party, the SDA or the Serbian Democratic Party, that we would most probably be able to do something, to meet with both sides, to see what the problem was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, before we discuss more about the League for Peace and what it did, I want to ask you a couple of questions about the circumstances at the time the League was formed. First of all, was the League for Peace organised after the takeover of Prijedor by Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware of a demand or ultimatum by Serbian authorities, by the new Serbian authorities, in Prijedor that Kozarac surrender weapons and that the police take an oath of allegiance to the new Serbian authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew of that ultimatum because they had forwarded it through the local community in Kozarac to the Party of Democratic Action asking for weapons to be surrendered, either legally or illegally obtained, so that the police, both the regular and extraordinary members, that is, the reservists, together with the Territorial Defence, should hand over their weapons to the army of Republika Srspka in Prijedor. I wish to point out that the Territorial Defence which numbered some 100 people had received weapons from that same Yugoslav Army. It had been equipped by that army. For six or seven months it had been active in Kozarac which was quite normal. Apparently, it was armed to avoid any incidents occurring. What kind of incidents they had in mind, I did not know because there were no incidents in Kozarac. However -- yes, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do not want to cut you off but that was a sufficient answer to the specific question I asked. I also wanted to ask you if at the time the League was formed you and the other members were aware of the gathering of Serbian troops and heavy weaponry in the area of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all knew. We all knew. This was no secret. The people in the villages, people in Kozarac, I also knew. I can mention that before going to my job to teach in the morning about 6.30 or 7.00, I personally counted 45 military trucks full of army, full of personnel. These were not young soldiers because they passed slowly through Kozarac. I counted one by one the trucks. They were unshaven people, irregularly dressed. They were dragging guns with the trucks, and on the cabin roofs they had machine guns installed. The canvas was lifted from the trucks and I could see that they were all armed. On the doors, not on all the doors of the trucks but on some of them, in red paint it said, "Wolves from Pakrac". That was the inscription. On the first truck a bull's head with horns was drawn, it was not drawn, the actual head was stuck to the truck so you could see the blood still running. So, believe me, this was shocking to me. They passed through Kozarac and they went off in the direction of Mrakovica. When I went to school, I talked to my colleagues. Everybody in Kozarac was aware of this and gradually we were swept by fear. Something was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The translation that we were given said that the trucks were "dragging guns". What kind of weapons were being towed by the military trucks you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not a military expert, but these were light cannon with two large wheels, one tube, I saw that, and each truck had one of these behind it. I could see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to Serb soldiers, were you aware of Serb civilians being armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must be sincere, I personally did not see armed Serb civilians, but the Muslim peasants living on the slopes of Mount Kozara would come to the Local Commune claiming that they had seen in Podgradje in the localities with the majority Serb population that the army was distributing weapons even to children and that every home was armed. We simply did not know why. We simply did not believe that this was happening and what for, for what reason. Kozarac at that time was sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who were the members of the group, the members of the League for Peace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The members of the League for Peace were independent people, people who were not affiliated with any party. They were not members of the SDA or any of the other parties. I was a member of the League for Peace. Hamdija Kahrimanovic, Nagib Mahmuljin, Dr. Pasic Jusuf, Jasim Fazlic, Hamdija Balic, Kemal Fazlic. Afterwards, as representatives for the League of Peace to have in our view some legitimacy, we asked representatives of other local communes, Kozarusa and Kamicani, to delegate people of Serb ethnicity, so that we should be homogenous, a mixed League, and on behalf of Kozarusa people proposed Djuro Pupevac, an older man, a fine man, and on behalf of Kamicani, Milenko Zigic. Unfortunately, this Milenko Zigic proved to have participated in the war operations in Kozarac, that he had committed a lot of evil. He stayed behind. Whether he is still alive, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you. This is a bit of an interruption, but I do not want to do this at the end, but I want to ask you a couple of questions about the members of the League whom you mentioned. Did Dr. Pasic survive the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Jasim Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jasim Fazlic was killed in a convoy moving in the direction of Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Hamdija Balic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hamdija Balic also disappeared in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about Nagib Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He also disappeared in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the League for Peace arrange a meeting with the Serbian authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the Local Commune, through a man called Nagib Mahmuljin, contact was established with the Serb authorities in Prijedor, and after a great deal of insistence on our part that we be received for talks to see what the problem was, because an aggression was obviously being prepared against Kozarac, they said they did not wish to receive a delegation of the SDA party. The reasons, I can only assume what were the reasons; only if an independent group would come, perhaps they would be ready to talk to them. We held a meeting at the school. Hamdija Kahrimanovic was present, and the idea occurred to me that if we go, regardless of the fact that we were not SDA members, after all we were Muslims, because the Serbs had already organised several checkpoints and we were not sure that we would be allowed to pass those checkpoints, so I proposed that we should have some Serbs with us, that that would be wise and normal because they too were people of Kozarac. They live in Kozarac. Kozarac is their place, their town too, and they should fight for Kozarac, just as we should in a normal democratic way. Then Hamdija asked me, "OK, who do you have in mind?" I had good relations with Dusko Tadic's family and so I said, "I propose Dusko Tadic". Hamdija said, "I do not believe he will be ready to go". We were still meeting there and I saw Dusko through the window and I said, "I am going straightaway to ask him". I asked him and, to be quite frank, he was not overenthusiastic about going, but he did say to me, "If you are going, I will go too". "OK", I said, "thank you". We exchanged a few more words. We were going to go to go tomorrow. I came in the morning to pick him up. He had changed his mind. He did not want to go. So I said, "Now that would not be really fair. You said you would go. You cannot back away now". So we went. We went by car to Prijedor. We were met there by repesentatives of the Serb army in Prijedor, and Simo Drljaca was already in uniform -- a man who had absolutely nothing to do with the army before. He was the secretary of our Centre for Elementary Education. He was in uniform. Radmilo Zeljaja, several officers whom I did not know. The minutes were kept by Pero Kovacevic, as far as I can remember, a man who was a principal of the Kozarac school for a time, afterwards he moved to Prijedor, and he worked in the communal administration. That does not matter anyway. We met there, maybe some 20 men in all. They received us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, excuse me, I want to make sure we identify who was there. In addition to Zeljaja and Mr. Drljaca, were other Serbian officials there and specifically was -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SDS in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry, sir, you were speaking but we were not receiving a translation. I do not know if there is a technical problem or not?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The answer says "SDS in Prijedor". You mean before that previous answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why do you not ask him again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, you had mentioned a couple of other Serbian officials who were present at the meeting in Prijedor, but we did not receive the translation. Can you repeat their names, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Radmilo Zeljaja was at the meeting, a man who was Commander of the military barracks in Prijedor; Slobodan Kuruzovic, Commander of the Trnopolje camp; Simo Miskovic, President of the SDS Party in Prijedor, and representatives of military authorities who were not familiar to me. They were wearing uniforms of the Yugoslav Army and, to be quite frank, they received us with some reserve. They were not friendly and we felt very awkward. We sat in a room. I had never been there before. It was probably a meeting place, a meeting room. The meeting started out without any proper order or any introduction. I can just say, if you wish, what the main aim was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do want to hear about that, I know the court does. Let me ask you first, however, did the members of the League for Peace come to make a specific proposal or for the purpose of discussing things generally and opening a dialogue and expressing their wish for peace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came to the first meeting, Kozarac was already blocked, nobody could leave Kozarac and we knew that the situation was highly problematic. We simply came to ask them what we should do, what the problem was, what had Kozarac done for them to ask us to give up legally obtained weapons; our hunters who had certificates to show that they had guns obtained early on or as security. The Federal Secretariat for Security in Prijedor had issued these certificates. They asked us to surrender all our weapons and that it should be stored in Prijedor. We were afraid of this, and we tried to find some kind of an alternative solution, but it was not possible to find any other solution except what they requested. They made it clear that their's was an ultimatum. We would either surrender our weapons or they would take them away themselves. In view of the fact that many towns in Bosnia had fallen according to the same scenarios, that many towns and villages had surrendered their weapons thinking that the army of Republika Srpska would act normally, however, they only facilitated their job for them. They entered, they set on fire, they killed, they raped, they took people to detention camps. So we knew that the same awaited us, whether we surrendered our weapons or not. If we had surrendered our weapons, we would have made it easier for them because they would know that none of their soldiers would get killed then. So we proposed that we would put our weapons away in the police station in Kozarac, and then have mixed guards to look after it, but to take it to Prijedor and to offer the people of Kozarac to the Serb paramilitary on a plate, as we say, no-one from the League of Peace felt authorised to do such a thing without asking the people of Kozarac. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. During that meeting, did any of the Serb leaders say that they had taken power in Prijedor because the Muslims planned a takeover and that the Muslims were planning to liquidate prominent Serbs and had marked the houses of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, this was another form of propaganda, so that -- so as to take power, the power over in Prijedor in a brutal way. The army of the Republika Srpska and the SDS removed the executives of the Party overnight who had been regularly elected and even though the majority of the population was Muslim, that we had simply gained more seats in the Municipal Assembly, in the court and so on and so forth, they were simply bothered by this and said they had to leave, that Muhamed Cuhajic could not be the Mayor of the municipality any longer and they took the power over by means of military force. It is not true, and I know it and I would have heard it, that anyone at any time marked Serb homes or compiled lists for the liquidation, for the elimination, of some Serbs. They did this to us because that is what turned out later, that is known. There are documents on that. During the war and in the camps at Keraterm and Trnopolje, in Omarska, they killed our intellectuals, prominent members of the SDA who had done absolutely nothing to bring about armed conflicts between Serbs and Muslims, and that is what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, did the Serbian leaders say to the League for Peace members at the meeting that that had happened and that was why they took power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, they were looking for, not a reason because there was no reason, but any ----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, I am probably not making the question clear. I simply want to know if that was said at the meeting or not, not what the reasons behind that propaganda might be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When the meeting was over did any of the Serbian leaders speak to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting ended in a very troublesome discussion, a very heavy atmosphere. As a matter of fact, we did nothing there. They also asked that our police puts on insignia of the army of the Republika Srpska and we had to take this proposal to Kozarac to explain that both to our police and to our people. However, when the meeting was over Simo Miskovic, President of the SDS, the man with whom I had grown up, stopped me and said, "Kemal, what you are doing are all of no use, nothing can save Kozarac". He also said, unless he was doing it to justify himself before me, that if I cannot do anything for Kozarac, then I will take my family and go to Belgrade. Simo did not go to Belgrade because I saw him in Omarska. Kozarac had already fallen. Kozarac had already been destroyed by then, and after a month, during the month when I was at the pista, Kozarac was burning day and night. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned Djuro Pupevac who was a member of a Local Commune who was a Serb. Did he speak up at the meeting on behalf of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Djuro Pupevac, as far as I could judge and some colleagues who were with me, Djuro Pupevac spoke very favourably. He is a man of modest scope, modest knowledge, but what he said was that in Kozarac there were no problem, that people of Serb origin did not have to fear anyone, that they could move freely, that they could go to work and that he did not understand why was Kozarac the place which was suddenly causing problems? He himself could not see what the problem was about. He raised this before the authorities of the Republika Srpska. There was no answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic speak up on behalf of Kozarac at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. He certainly was with us but I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic tell you that he had met with the Serbian leaders immediately before the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic tell you that he was going to talk with Serbian leaders immediately before the meeting, or did he tell you sometime afterwards that he had talked with the Serbian leaders immediately before the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he said that he would talk to Serb leaders, I would not know with whom specifically, he did not mention any name, and whether he did, whether he did talk to someone, I do not know. I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps had I paid more attention to that during all that, perhaps I might have learned whether he had done that or not. But after that there was nothing to tell me that it had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he tell whether he regarded the meeting as potentially useful or as a waste of time before it had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regrettably, his comment was almost identical to Simo Miskovic's one. After that meeting I went to his coffee bar. We sat down, had some juice and he said, "Kemal, Kozarac is going to be shelled". I was shocked. I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry. I did not mean to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there a second meeting a few days before the attack on Kozarac in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was another meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it attended by basically the same people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More or less. However, this meeting was hardly different from that first one. The status quo continued because no one side, neither of the sides could or wanted to make a single concession. Serbs on one side because they were demanding that the arms be turned over, that our police put their insignia on; we on the other side in Kozarac did not absolutely want to turn over those few weapons which we had, to turn them into their hands and to be at the mercy of those people who had come to Kozarac and attack us, because we knew that because it already happened in too many places around Bosnia. Sarajevo was on fire already at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were the results of those two meetings and ultimatum by the Serbian authorities communicated to the people of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were communicated. After the second meeting, we organised a citizens' meeting, rally, in our hall. It was filled to capacity. All the people that could get in did get in, and we explained to our townsmen what we were being asked for, and we asked the citizenry to decide because they were the only ones authorised to do such a thing. They then cast vote and indicated that they did not want to surrender their weapons and fall bare-handed in the arms of Serb soldiers because they thought it would be fatal. That was the answer of Kozarac people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Kozarac in a position to defend itself militarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDA and the League for Peace at a meeting set up jointly a Crisis Committee, what we called that. There were about 10 people there, and we had all the information, what kind of weapons there were in Kozarac and what could we use to defend ourselves if we were attacked by the Serb army. To be quite frank, to make, to draw a comparison, it was David and Goliath game, because what we had were mostly hunting rifles. The automatic rifles, they were had by the police, the regular and the Reserve Police. Old hunting rifles and very old ones were in the hands of the Territorial Defence, but they were practically unusable, those rifles. Some, perhaps, had a pistol or a revolver and that is all that I knew about. So at one of the meetings I asked a man who had undertaken to organise some kind of defence of Kozarac, how to organise if Kozarac were attacked, Sead Cirkin. So I asked, "Sead, how much ammunition do we have if we are attacked?" and he said, "We have ammunition to last us for two hours of fighting", and I laughed then and he asked me, "Why do you laugh?" "Sead, we are finished. Do you know, Sead, what kind of force they are bringing against us? There are cannon, heavy guns in Mrakovica, heavy trucks are there. Around Prijedor, the place is called Crna Dolina, and their tanks are positioned there. Kozarusa, there are also tanks positioned. There is no way out for us. There is no chance of escaping that", and we all knew that, but we could not and we should not have left our women, our children, our old folk, at the mercy of Serbs who would come to Kozarac, and we knew they would come, because on 23rd May, on Saturday already, the village of Hambarine was set on fire, was burning. We saw that from Kozarac. Everything was burnt down. People were killed. At that time, even at that time, Omarska was a topical matter. Keraterm was already open.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were in Kozarac when the attack began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you spend two days and two nights in the centre of Kozarac in a basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I and my family and a large number of Kozarac inhabitants from the heart of the town which we call Carsija, hid in the cellar of the building across the building in which I lived. There was a subsidiary of the Privredna Bank of Sarajevo and with our families we hid there. We organised ourselves a little, had some food, had some blankets with us, believing that after that shelling they were preparing for us after two or three days some kind of truce would be there. There would not be a full scale war. We thought it would last for a couple of days and then we would be able to come up with a solution, but something completely different happened. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the third day when people from Kozarac began to surrender in columns, you and your family joined the column and went to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shelling lasted for two days and two nights from Sunday to Tuesday morning, May 26th. On the radio station, the army of the Republika Srpska communicated that all the Kozarac people had to surrender, and that those who did not would be liquidated, regardless whether we had any weapons or not, that we had to take out white flags and form an echelon and leave from Kozarac to the highway Prijedor/Banja Luka taking the direction of Prijedor. So we set off. But only those who were in the centre of the town set off. A great many people who lived on the outskirts, in the villages, they stayed because they knew nothing about that. They stayed, unfortunately, because very many were killed. We reached the highway towards Prijedor. We then reached a bus station. There we were met by soldiers of the Republika Srpska and I heard it with my own ears how they shouted, fire, beat, kill them, do not wait anything. We heard our mothers, our children and we were bare handed. I could not believe my ears. I could not believe that this man was saying things like that. I was wondering why. Another one was saying, "No, wait, we have not received our orders yet". So there was quite a confusion among them and we were slowly moving towards Kozarusa and there we were met by buses. We saw a large number of tanks, very many men, troops there, and guns and cannons. They were heavily armed, thinking that Kozarac would put up resistance. However, Kozarac absolutely had no chance, had no opportunity to resist them. Kozarac had simply hidden before them. So we came down, women and children, and then they started separating them from men or minor boys, boys of 12 or 13. In the crudest way possible, in the most brutal way possible, they put us on to the buses and took us by the old road towards Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you able to leave Trnopolje on that same day with the assistance of a colleague of your sister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived in Trnopolje and the situation there was very hard. My younger sister at the time was employed in the Secretariat for the Interior in Prijedor. She had her boyfriend who was a Serb, so he approached him and asked him if it will be possible for her family and mine to leave Trnopolje because we were afraid. We realised that some ugly things would happen there and he said to wait. So he found a small truck and we boarded that one and headed for Prijedor. So, that night we spent with friends again, and the next day my family went to the old town in Prijedor, to some relatives of mine, somewhat removed. There we were until the fatal May 30th, the morning when Prijedor and Stari Grad were attacked, when that Stari Grad, when old town was burnt to the ground and that is when they took us to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify. You were taken to Trnopolje on one bus, your wife and children were taken on another bus and then you met in Trnopolje with the assistance of this friend and were taken to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, upon our arrival in Trnopolje, the army separated men from women and put them into an old hall, a cinema. It is the same kind of a hall as the one in Kozarac except that it is slightly older and that is where they put us. However, when some fire started, some uncontrolled, I think, some random fire, we were scared because we thought that they were firing at our women and children. So we all rushed out of that hall and that is how we got mixed again with the women and children. After that they did not try particularly hard to put us back, but started to accommodate us around the school rooms in that old school in Trnopolje. There we found that man and then left for Prijedor and it was around sunset, it was dusk already, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You say you were in Stari Grad on May 30th when the cleansing of Stari Grad began. Did that begin with shelling in the early morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attack on Stari Grad started in the morning of May 30th. First, one could hear individual pistol shots and then it grew stronger and stronger and we realised something was happening. The houses began to burn, and then into those small streets in the old town so-called Pitzgauers, military vehicles, entered with soldiers on and they had machine guns on them, and they were firing at buildings and houses, absolutely wanton fire. They did not check whether there were any women or old people or children. Then they started entering houses, breaking into homes. They were asking for keys of the cars. Women were taking off whatever jewellery they had, so they were looting, they were pillaging. They were taking money and telling us all, "Leave all that is valuable. Just leave it behind. You will not need it any more". They would not even allow us to dress. My wife left the house bare footed, and not only I, but everybody else as well. So they made us move towards the Balkan Hotel. There they separated us once again, women from men, brought a large number of buses and with those buses we were taken to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Omarska where were you first held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see this model of Omarska. We were brought by buses here, to this administrative building, and for the first three or four days I was in one of those rooms in the back. We entered through this main entrance. One goes into the restaurant a soldier met us one by one and took down our first names and family names. There were incredibly many of us in that room. One could hardly breathe. So that at our own initiative we started to look for some other rooms. People were opening doors and going into other rooms, and then the orders came that we all had to abandon those rooms and that we had to go out to the asphalted space which, I do not know for what reason, was called "pista". Why is it called pista? I do not know to this day, and it does not matter anyway, but that is the name which we also adopted and I spent a month on that pista. We spent that day and night, we even slept there. In the rain or not, when it rained, if it was cold, if there was puddles of water, we still had to lie there. We could not even crouch or stand up because if you stand up, we were all surrounded by amoured vehicles of the army of the Republika Srpska, there were machine guns which fired over our heads, so we simply had to lie down. We were terribly cold. So we tried to be close to each other. Some elderly people cried. There were children too. It was very hard. During the first five days and five days they would not -- they gave us nothing to eat, nor did they give us any water to drink. We were physically crushed. When we did have an opportunity to stand up, which was not very often allowed, many people fainted. Simply, you would see all dark in front of you. You either had to grab the one next to you or fall down. It is unimaginable. We could not speak. My lips were all parched. I was bleeding. I could not understand that a man was doing this on to a man that people with whom we had worked together, played together, could do this, married with, went to funerals together, attended funerals together. It was terribly hard. I mean it was hard on our souls. We were terribly affected. We really found it very hard on us, believe me. I do not really want to tax your patience with these stories, so if you have any questions, of course, I will listen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think this is actually a time for a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Susic, you were on the pista area for approximately one month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then you were transferred to the large hangar building which is also shown on the model?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you first on the ground floor of the hangar building in an enclosed area on the floor of the hangar where large mine equipment was normally kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That area was fenced in with wire where the prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At some point after that, did you manage to sneak away from that area and get to a room in the upstairs portion of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I managed to get out. When we entered the hangar -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The transcript is not appearing -- it appears to be operative. Mr. Tieger, you need to begin again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, I am going to ask you the same questions I asked you a few moments ago because the transcription of what you were saying was not appearing. You were on the pista for about a month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After that you were transferred to the large hangar building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were held with other prisoners on the floor of the hangar building in an area where the large mining equipment was normally kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All prisoners from the pista were transferred to the hangar. Old mining machinery that was inoperative was thrown out. We were put there and wired in. I spent several days there. I did my best to get away as soon as possible because every evening soldiers would come, take men away, kill them, beat them up heavily, and seeing that my life was in danger, I sought an alternative solution and one occasion when the electricity failed, I managed to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You went into a room in the upstairs portion of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You remained there until the time of your transfer to Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the time you were in Omarska were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interrogated only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know the person who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. His name was Dragan Radakovic, with several other men that I did not know. In addition to him there were two soldiers of the Republika Srpska who with beatings forced the detainees to give them information they wanted to hear. The treatment was very cruel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you beaten during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see the conditions of other prisoners before and after their interrogations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see that. When I was taken for interrogation I was at the pista at the time. Mostly when interrogations occurred we were asked to face the hangar so as not to see the condition in which people were coming out after interrogation. They were severely beaten up, so they sought a jacket or a blanket to be brought upstairs so that the beaten up person, even those who gave no sign of life, to be taken out, to be laid down on the grass in front of the restaurant. This happened daily. Things like this happened daily. In the case of my interrogation, a soldier called Milan Pavlic approached me, put a bayonet under my throat, he threatened me saying that I must answer the questions put to me by Mr. Radakovic, and afterwards he asked me, "How do you want me to cut your throat?" I said, "In the way that it is easier for you". Then Radakovic gave him a sign with his eyes to let me go and told me to go back to the pista, that he would think about me, but that most probably I and my two brothers would be liquidated. Why, I did not know. I returned to the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated before the prisoners were beaten on occasions other than interrogations. Did you see the condition of prisoners who were held in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The white house was for us a kind of purgatory. People would go there but they were carried out severely beaten up and in most cases already dead. The knowledge that you would have to go to the white house was terrible, because if they told you you had to go there, it would in most cases mean the end. I saw those people that were beaten up, that were maimed, with open fractures of their extremities, their limbs, their arms and legs with severe injuries on the face so that some people I had known I could no longer recognise. One of those people was the President of the SDA party in Kozarac, Becir Medunjanin. He was severely beaten up as well as his son who survived, in roughly about that time he was liquidated in Omarska. He begged the soldier to kill him, just not to beat him any more. I heard this myself, and I watched it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any Serbian officials from Prijedor in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Omarska on a couple of occasions I saw Simo Miskovic and Simo Drljaca. I saw the two of them in broad daylight. Simo Drljaca was wearing a camouflage uniform. He knew and saw what was happening, the kind of treatment we were exposed to. I believe he did nothing to help or change the situation because the situation remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was the Commander of Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Commander of the Omarska camp was Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see Simo Drljaca talking with Zeljko Meakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually, when Simo came to Omarska at the very entrance to the building or the restaurant, he was met by Mejakic or a number of the officers with whom he would have a five-minute talk outside and then he would go upstairs. They had their own offices upstairs where they probably discussed future activities and developments. I do not know about that, but I saw them talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did officials, Serbian officials, from outside Prijedor come to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Representatives of Serb authorities outside Prijedor, I can mention a specific case of Radoslav Brdjanin, a man who was the pillar of the SDS party in Banja Luka. He came on one occasion by helicopter. I remember well the helicopter landed just behind the restaurant building. The man came out. Everybody said it was Radoslav Brdjanin. He introduced himself later on. We were lined up and we were ordered to sing Chetnik songs. Many people, so as not to be killed, sang and cried. At the end he said to us with a lot of sarcasm, "Why did you need all this?" and Kozarac by then had already been destroyed and burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the time you were held in Omarska camp, did you see Dusko Tadic in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, in view of all the developments before the war, the fact that I knew the family, I personally would have liked not to have seen him. I saw Dusko Tadic only once in Omarska. He came with a group of soldiers of the Republika Srspka. When I saw him that day, it was a sunny, light day. Dusko was not carrying weapons. I did not see any weapons on him. He was talking to some people. He entered the administrative building and went upstairs because I was sitting on the pista then, and then through the glass you can see the people climbing up the stairs or coming down the stairs. That day I did not see him coming down. In the evening, those of us on the pista were obliged to leave the pista and we were put, 600 or 700 of us, in the restaurant to spend the night because it was easier for them to keep check of us, so that no-one could get away or make an incident or anything. It was terrible for us because we were one on top of the other. We could not breathe. At the same time they would come in and beat us up or take some away somewhere, we did not know where. We would spend the night. In the morning we would go back to the pista again and spend the whole day there until the moment when we left it. I am talking of the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am going to ask you to stand up in just a moment and point out the spot where you were sitting on the pista when you saw Dusko Tadic, and then also point out the spot where he was when you first saw him. I will also ask you -- perhaps you can take that pointer with you -- can you first point out the spot on the pista where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This area here between the administrative building and the restaurant and this building where the offices were, the offices of the hangar. We, prisoners, called it the "pista". It was limited with flower pots we were ordered not to go beyond, and this area behind was also used when we were lined up for lunch, that infamous lunch. Dusko was coming along this side. I was here somewhere, roughly. It was in broad daylight. The weather was sunny and I could not have replaced him for someone else. He moved slowly, talking with some soldiers and he entered here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you put a couple of yellow tabs which I believe are on the model, left side of the model, and should be marked "T" and "W" -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Sutherland, it might be better if the witness uses those earphones and he will be able to move further over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Using the tab marked "W", can you place that in the approximate area where you were when you first saw Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, we can barely hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, if you are going to speak, you will have to be a little closer to the microphone for the interpreters to hear what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. This tab with "W" shows where I was roughly. It is very difficult to say exactly -- roughly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you use the marker that is marked with a "T" to show approximately where Dusko Tadic was when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko was about here somewhere. He was moving, I think, from here. I could not see. I did not pay any attention until he appeared. This part here and this part is in glass, so that it is possible to see this side through the glass. Whether he was a little more forward or backward, but roughly here somewhere. I did not pay attention to the actual distance because, of course, I did not think about such things at the time. He was moving slowly, talking all the time, and noticing him, in view of our mutual friendly relationships from before, I spontaneously raised my hand in a wish to give him a sign to tell him I was there, hoping that he could help me. My brother-in-law was sitting next to me. He pulled my hand down and said, "Don't do that, Kemal. You do not know what could happen to you". These mixed feelings and being disappointed, I lowered my hand. I sometimes think about that event, perhaps Dusko maybe even noticed me, but he gave no sign of it, no real sign of recognition and he went in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, you can resume your seat now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How were the soldiers who were with Dusko Tadic dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time the army of the Republika Srpska had diverse uniform. Some were wearing camouflage pants and ordinary jackets of the former Yugoslav People's Army, some wearing blue shirts, some were wearing civilian clothes. They were very disorderly, unshaven. According to my judgment, it was an army without discipline, without order. They behaved like hooligans. They were swearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How were these particular soldiers with Mr. Tadic dressed, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were also dressed differently. They were armed with automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you recall, how was Dusko Tadic dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko had camouflage pants and a shirt without a jacket. He was not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Camouflage shirt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, an ordinary shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated that he and the people he was with moved slowly across the front of the restaurant building and then entered the restaurant building. Were you able to see him going upstairs through the glass on the stairway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was because the glass panes were very visible and the whole part was in glass, maybe plastic glass, I do not know, so that anyone climbing or descending the stairs could be seen well and one could easily tell who was who. It was not a large distance. They would often have three or four people there observing the people on the pista to see who was sitting with whom, who was communicating with whom, whether there were any connections among the people. In a certain area from the restaurant there was a point with a man with a machine gun who was guarding the people sitting on the pista. These are just some details. I do not know whether they are important. I just want to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You remained on the pista until darkness when you were put in the restaurant building, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the day you saw Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You did not see him leave the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, can you look around the courtroom, please, and tell us if Dusko Tadic is in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you point him out, please, and tell us what he is wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the man sitting in the middle. He has a blue jacket, a tie and a white shirt.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, I first of all want to ask you some questions about the time before Kozarac was attacked. You have told us about you being involved with the peace group who went to Prijedor to negotiate on behalf of Kozarac. You told us that Dusko Tadic was a member of that group when you went on the two occasions. You recollect your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You also told us that it was your idea to suggest him to the group and that you happened to leave the room that you were in because you saw him on the street outside and put the idea to him. Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect, before you spoke to him about those arrangements, whether, in fact, there had previously been discussions between you and he about this meeting in Prijedor to meet members of the Crisis Staff there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect, in fact, also at one of those meetings did Bosko Dragicevic also accompany you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosko Dragicevic was proposed to go with us. However, he refused, he did not want to go with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Present at the meeting in Prijedor was there a man called Mehmet Ilijaz who was President of the SDA in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mehmet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mehmet Ilijaz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not accompanying your delegation, but being someone from Prijedor who was also there with the other people from Prijedor, some of whom you have named? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- please? At that meeting, Dedo Trnalic was present, as far as I remember. I am not an inhabitant of Prijedor. I do not know many people from Prijedor. What is more, I knew very few people who were linked to the SDA party in Prijedor, so that I cannot give you reliable information on the names of the people attending that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as that meeting was concerned, do you recollect if any notes were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, notes were being taken by a man called Pero Kovacevic. On what basis he was entrusted with this task, I do not know. I think that he was doing that, however. Those notes were not given to us to see what had been taken down. This was simply taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just a couple of other matters prior to the attack on Kozarac: I do not know whether you recollect a man who used to live in Kozarac called Adem Kahrimanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before the attack took place on Kozarac, is it right that he moved to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect, in fact, if he went to stay with his sister in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he went with his wife and he went to stay with my sister in Banja Luka who was then living in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, you are probably right about that and I am interpreting something that is given to me and I accept what you said. It was with your sister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. That is true. That man is my uncle and his wife my aunt, and they lived with my sister in Banja Luka for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect, in fact, that Dusko Tadic as well as his brother Ljubo helped Adem to move from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That they had helped him directly, they did not, but Dusko did advise him that it would be wise to leave Kozarac probably knowing what could happen to Kozarac; most probably again out of gratitude because that man had lent him a certain sum of money to complete his building and my uncle went to Banja Luka. I personally drove him to the junction with the main road Prijedor/Banja Luka, and he went to Banja Luka by bus from there and he stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you hear from Adem at all during the time that you were either at Trnopolje or Omarska? Did you have any messages from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Trnopolje for only one day until dusk. In Omarska I spent two months and seven days. I never received any message from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to deal with some other matters as well concerning Dusko Tadic. First of all, you are a man who has always worn a beard, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not so frequently. I would shave sometimes but sometimes it was like a fashion, a fad, and I thought there was nothing bad to wear a beard, for me to wear a beard is a normal thing, a democratic choice of any individual. Everyone is free to clothe as he will or to wear a beard if he wants to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was not criticising it!

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand you to be criticising. I just thought I owed you an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, but as part of your democratic choice I suppose you also had to carry an identification card, is that right, in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that identification card would be the photograph of the person who was the bearer of the card? The translation needs to pick up your answer rather than nodding, sir. If you can answer yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I will tell you. I am listening to you. I had an ID card. I still have it with me in [redacted] I can show you the photograph. On that photograph I wore a beard as a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My question was not actually proposed to be about that, but if you changed your appearance having not worn a beard but then started to wear a beard on a more permanent basis, is it correct that you had to change the photograph inside the identification card?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the rules, yes, but our authorities in Bosnia were not so strict, especially in the locality where we were living. It was sufficient to show our ID card. Whether we were clean shaven or with a beard they knew my identity and who I was and that everything was in order. There were no sanctions or consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As far as Dusko Tadic was concerned, you have referred to whether he had a beard or not, but can you recollect that there was in fact a period shortly before the conflict in 1992 when he did have a permanent full beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have known him, as you have told the Court, for many years. There were times, though, in fact when he had lived away from Kozarac, perhaps the 1980s you may remember that he went to Libya, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do not know whether he was in Libya, but I do know for a while he was not in Kozarac and I know he spent some time in Banja Luka. But, believe me, this is the first time I hear that he had lived in Libya. Kozarac is a small place, perhaps I would have heard of that, but, after all, I do not think it is particularly important and why should I or somebody else know if Dusko Tadic was in Libya or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What it comes to is this, though, that you recollect that there were periods when he lived away from Kozarac; where he was living you cannot say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he lived in Banja Luka because he had a car with Banja Luka plates of Visa make. I think I can even remember the colour of his car. It was a grey colour. He would frequently come with that car to Kozarac and then he would go to Banja Luka. What he did in Banja Luka I do not and, after all, it is really his private business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Aside of that period in Banja Luka, do you in fact recollect him working elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia in a different region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. I only know that he often went to Germany to his brother Mladen who lived in Munich at the time.
