Whether he worked in Germany or did something in Germany or not, whether he had a regular job there, I do not know that either, but I think not, since I saw him often enough and those visits of his were usually of a short duration. So he often was in Kozarac and he mostly moved between Banja Luka and Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect in fact, again before the attack on Kozarac, that he had put on a lot of weight, he was heavier than he had been in the past?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. I remember that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You would notice those changes in how he looked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I noticed that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, he is not someone that you used to see dressed in army clothes. That was not the kind of clothing that you would have seen him wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war I did not see him wearing that uniform in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether somebody else saw him in it I do not know, but I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, when you saw him he would be wearing just ordinary clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I would like now to ask you some questions about Trnopolje and the first one is one of enquiry. You mentioned being helped in Trnopolje by someone called Bozo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think his name was Bozo and that man worked, as far as I know from what my sister told me, for the Secretariat of the Interior in Prijedor. I think that at the time he was already retired, but when the war broke out he had been reactivated. What his family name is I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that Bozo Karajica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karajica or Karajica, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One other matter. When you were in Omarska did you receive food from a guard who helped you called Merko Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all I ask about those matters and I now want to go to the occasion you were on the pista. You say that you saw Dusko Tadic. Can you recollect when that was, how long you had been at Omarska by that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was brought to Omarska on May 30th '92, and to be able to specify the date when I saw him, at that time I thought -- no, I did not even give it a thought at the time, but I should say it was sometime in June, I should say the latter half of June. It was relatively warm at the time. It must have been around noon. It was sunny. We were all sitting on the pista facing -- well, it depended. We were slightly relaxed at that particular moment and it just happened that I was facing the restaurant, the administrative building, more out of curiosity because many things were going on in front of that entrance. New people came, new prisoners were brought, they were beaten at that entrance and distributed around different rooms and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that the time when you stayed the night in the hangar or the restaurant building or when you were out on the pista during the night time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time by and large we would spend the whole evening and often every, all the evenings we stayed outside, but often for security reasons they forced us to enter the restaurant because that was how they could keep the eye on us easier. Then we would be thrown out in the morning at 6 or half past, we would be thrown out and each of us looked for a place on the pista to take up for the day. I do not know what you have in mind, but it is absolutely impossible of a mistaken personality. I could have perhaps been wrong about someone whom I had known for a month or two, but for somebody who grew up before my eyes, who was my pupil, whose walk, whose characteristic walk, characteristic step I knew, whose gestures I knew, whose manner of speech I knew, it was very hard to be mistaken about such a person. To be quite frank, his appearance there was a great disappointment to me personally because I thought he would distance himself from this or at least that he would not come to Omarska which was the evil itself, and it was proven in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, what I suggest to you is that a mistaken person such as you can believe their mistake, and that is what I suggest, that you are mistaken about this identification. Perhaps you would like me now to look at some of the details with you whilst I ask some questions so that we can judge this matter. You referred to flower pots between the ----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I am sorry to interrupt you, but before we get too close I want to ask for a redaction on the time delay.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What do you mean a redaction on the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is a reference earlier in the transcript and it occurs at 12.31.32 on page 41/15. So if that could be communicated to the technicians.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What time did it occur, 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It refers to a location the Court may recall.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What time did it occur?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Is there any objection -- do you have that on your screen, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have been told by Miss de Bertodano what the matter is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Look and you will see at 12.31.32, the location. No objection to it being redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good, it will be redacted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Can I then ask you about certain details concerning this matter. The first is this, that you mentioned flower pots that existed as a boundary on the pista. Were they placed like a channel between both of the sides of the hangar stretching down to the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were flower pots and they looked nothing like a channel. They were simply put there as a decoration, and formerly there were flowers in them. I should like to ask you to explain to me why do you infer and also to show me a document and on the basis of what do you draw your conclusion that I mistook him for another person and could I make this mistake? This is what you told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Please, I think that things will proceed more easily for the Court if you allow me to ask the questions and you answer the questions I ask you. Then if any other matters need to be raised by Prosecution counsel they will do so. So, if you just, please, answer my questions we shall not be very long. All I wanted to know was the position of the flower pots that you said bounded the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to stand up to show it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Please do so and if Mr. Bos can give you the pointer just mark where these pots were so that we can see you in court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (The witness indicated on the model). I do not know how many of them there were exactly, but this is how they were towards the restaurant and on the other side. True, of course, there was room between them, there was a certain space between them, so one could walk between them and we who were on the pista were ordered not to leave the area beyond the flower pots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you for answering my enquiry and you can return to your seat. What I would like to ask you now is if you can tell us about how many people were on that pista with you in June, are you able to give us a number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would I be right in suggesting that that is a very crowded area for 600 people to have been placed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are quite right. They were packed men next to men. It was very crowded. We could not move but we had to be there. We had been ordered not to leave that area. There was barely room to sit one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During the day were you required to either lie down or sit down and on a few occasions were you allowed to stand up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Often times when soldiers would come from the frontline, when they beat people up severely and killed them, we would then be ordered to lie down faced to the asphalt and we were often one on top of the other, but we could not raise our heads to see who were those people who were taking people away and killing them following a certain scenario, following ready-made lists. We were not allowed to see that. It was enough for a soldier to come up to you and ask you: "Do you know me?" If you said you did you are killed. We would lie in water for five or six hours and we would not be allowed to stand up. If it rained the whole day we were not allowed to move away, so our clothes got soaked and dried on us. It was very hard to lie down. When we were ordered to get up very many people remained lying down. Some elderly people died on the pista because they had already been emaciated, exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it the case that on an ordinary day you were required to sit down on the pista with your heads facing the tarmac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked that on several occasions. Usually and more often than not in the day time when the Commission from Banja Luka, on those days when the Banja Luka Commission came to conduct interrogations, some inspectors who came and some police from the Secretariat of the Interior would take people to the upper floor of the restaurant building, and after those infamous interrogations, during those infamous interrogations of theirs they heavily beat our people, battered them, and we were ordered not to look in that direction, so either to sit down facing in the opposite direction towards another building, or to lie face down to the asphalt. It was enough for one to raise one's head for soldiers, dozens of them, to start running over our backs in their soldiers' boots, to hit us with diverse objects, with metal, iron rods, with cables or whatever they could find. It was enough for one to raise one's head and receive a terrible blow in the head and it happened very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So are you saying then when nothing in particular was happening in the form of a beating or to disguise who was present at the camp, that in those circumstances you were able to look up and around and did not have to face the ground or the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When there was a relative lull, well, no excesses happened, then we were allowed to sit down facing one another or ask for water. Sometimes we were allowed to drink water from the nearby river which they brought in petrol cans. That water was undrinkable, it was full of insects or mud, but we had to drink it because there was no other water for us. Those were the only moments when we were, so to speak, relatively relaxed or in slight fear, but that happened very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it seems then on that one occasion when you say you saw Dusko Tadic that that was an occasion when you were able to look around, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, then we were free at that moment. We could perhaps walk a little bit, move among us or if somebody had some food over, perhaps biscuits or a small piece of bread after lunch, we had it in our pockets, in the jackets or something, so that at that moment I was facing the restaurant and we often faced the restaurant to see if somebody might bring our friends or relatives or brothers, our wives, mothers, and they did do that. In Omarska some 40 women were brought and they went through the severest treatment and we saw that, we heard that. I cannot ever forget the screams by night and the sobs, the cries for help. In the morning as they would sit in the restaurant at the table I saw there were bruises on their eyes and with the signs of blows, with clothes torn. Those were women who could not utter a single word, they did not cry even. Their faces were white and they stared in some direction, which one, they were completely lost. It was terrible to look at. We on one side all beaten up and maimed and they on the other. These are facts. These are the documents about Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So on this occasion we are talking about, no one had caused you or the other people with you to have to look in any other direction to stop you seeing anything happening or protect anyone's identity, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked, the soldiers from the frontline often came in combat vehicles, furious, vengeful and they asked that we turn towards the hangar and they would come in amongst us and those who were slightly stronger, who had not lost too much weight, they took away, beat up severely and many of them did not return. There were also such moments, and frequent ones too, when they were taken to the white house and from the white house they returned as invalids, totally disabled or were taken out dead and laid down on the grass in front of the white house. Every morning a yellow truck with an improvised excavator took those people to where the turnings of the mine were. Some of those people even still gave sign of life, they were not dead, yet they took them away and buried them alive. It is not only I who knows that. Very many people know it and many people would confirm that it was like that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, I think the question is, was there anything that interfered with your view, your ability to see Mr. Tadic. Was that the question, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Expressed in a slightly different way.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you wish you may restate the question. I do not see an answer to it, that is the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, you need an answer. I think you deserve an answer on this question. The point was, I do not think it was answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am much obliged. (To the witness): What I am asking you about is that on this occasion that you say you saw Dusko Tadic you had no order to turn to the hangar or look to the ground, so you could not see who was there or what was happening, is that right? A simple answer will probably help the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Explanation, I will tell you. When I saw Dusko nothing particular was happening on the pista. There were no incidents there, so that none of the superiors had ordered us to face the hangar or take up a particular posture so as not to see something. He simply turned up accompanied by several men, passed by and entered the restaurant building. We simply recorded that nothing happened, there was no problem, no incident, because they did not think there was anything terrible, anything bad was happening so that we would have to turn towards the building of the restaurant or turn away from the building of the restaurant. I do not know if I answered your question, but that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, cross-examination has not been completed of this witness. Yesterday when we enquired of how much time Mr. Wladimiroff would need for his presentation on the identification question, he had said an hour, I guess a half an hour as I recall, I have not looked at my notes, half an hour for himself and perhaps another half hour for Dr. Wagenaar if he is available. Is Dr. Wagenaar available?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Professor Wagenaar will be available for between 4 and 4.30. Arrangements were made last night so that he could attend the court. So he will be here from 4 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He will be here in this courtroom testifying from 4 to 4.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is what we are hoping, your Honour. He is arriving between 4 and 4.30. He has just come back from overseas, as the Court was told.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The point is, I do not think we will need two hours to hear argument on this point either from the Defence or the Prosecution. Maybe we will. In any case, since we have not completed cross-examination with this witness you may release your other witnesses, Mr. Tieger. We will continue and complete Mr. Susic and then we will hear argument on the identification question. If we finish early we will probably find something we can do with that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was hoping to be fairly brief to finish with this witness, your Honour. I was not intending to be a great -- I had hoped to finish before lunch but I was not intending to be much longer.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will leave it at that. You may dismiss your remaining witnesses. When we finish with Mr. Susic we will then hear argument and decide how we are going to proceed on this other issue and then adjourn because of the need of this courtroom for the other Trial Chamber. Very good. We will stand in recess then until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at 4 o'clock this afternoon I have another matter that I have to attend to and I wonder if I might be excused?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay? MR. KEMAL SUSIC, recalled Cross-examined by MR. KAY, continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, just a few more questions: going back to that time that you say you saw Dusko Tadic whilst you were on the pista at Omarska, can you describe what his appearance was like on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can. On that occasion Tadic was wearing a camouflage military pants and a shirt without a jacket. He had no weapons on him. Several people escorting him were carrying weapons. They were carrying automatic rifles or a pistol at their belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What about his facial appearance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean whether he was bearing a beard or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not wearing a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he clean shaven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one other matter that I want to ask you. In your time that you have known Dusko Tadic, have you ever seen him riding a motor bike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war or?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, before the war.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see you moving. I will overrule your objection. You may proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. I have not seen Dusko riding a motor cycle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. I have one question, Mr. Susic, I think, if I can find it. How long were you in Omarska, Mr. Susic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Omarska two months and seven days. From May 30th when I was brought there until August 7th when we were transferred to Manjaca, into a military war camp.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, additional questions, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Susic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I had indicated before our recess a few days ago that we would now hear argument on a submission by the Defence to exclude testimony on identification of witnesses who have been shown a photospread by the Prosecution. We have received that submission as well as the attachment, an article by William A. Wagenaar and the Prosecutor has filed its response yesterday evening. Is the Defence ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before we hear argument from the Defence, Mr. Tieger, I would like you, please, to explain how you intend to use this photospread evidence. It is still not clear to the Trial Chamber exactly how you will use it. I think we understand that there is a photospread, photos, consisting of 13 individuals -- is it 13?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That these were then shown to 39 persons. The question becomes if you then show the photospread to an individual, if you did, and that individual made an identification, how do you intend to utilize the identification in court? What are you going to do? What are you going to ask the witness and what reliance will you place on his or her previous selection or non-selection? That would be helpful just to lay the ground work for us. There may be additional questions from Judge Stephen. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe the answer to your question, your Honour, depends on the particular witness involved. So let me discuss the categories of witnesses individually. First of all, with respect to what I might term a classic identification witness, that is, someone who did not know the accused prior to the incident in question and has no way of identifying the accused other than either being shown the accused or shown a photograph of the accused, and in such a case a witness who is then presented with a series of photographs and asked if he or she recognises anyone in those photographs and points to a particular photograph and says, "Yes, that is the person involved in that particular incident", one may then reasonably conclude that that selection is based on the single prior contact with that particular person. In such a case, although we have not discussed it and I do not believe it is the subject of the Defence's concern, there are, presumably, two ways of eliciting that particular selection. One is through the witness and to have him recount his selection of the photograph and the circumstances in which it occurred. The other, presumably, would be to have the investigator who conducted the interview in which the selection was made describe what happened. As I say, it is not my understanding that that has been the focus of the Defence concern. Their issue has been the photographs themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In your response you, though, have identified -- you focus on the need to make sure that the process itself is fair and cite Biggers, Manson and Denno -- there are a lot of Denno's, I forget the other name. So that is the process. Suppose, though, that a person did know the accused before, do you intend to show the photospread to those witnesses and then how would you use that testimony? Specifically, would you merely want the witness to testify, yes, he knew him before, and then you would enquire of how he knew him and what was the contact? Then you would want the person to identify in the photospread if he or she had made a selection, but would you also want that witness to identify the accused in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would think if the Prosecution chose to elicit evidence of the selection of the accused from the photo line-up, although I do not know that -- in any event, yes, I think again both of those factors go to the weight to be given to the particular recognition. I think they are both appropriate. Clearly, one does not preclude the other. I cite as a specific example the witness we had before us earlier who made an in-court identification of the accused whom he knew from long before, and whose previous selection of the accused's photograph from a photo line-up was elicited in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is it your position that this second proposition, that is, if someone knew the person before and you have used the photospread and you then want them to testify about their identification during the photospread while they were looking at the photospread, is this identification or is it this recognition or is there a difference? Maybe we are getting too deeply into your argument. Maybe I have asked you enough to lay the ground work, have I?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you wish an answer, your Honour, there is no problem. I think, for discussion purposes in particular it is useful to distinguish between what we are starting to call identification and what may be called recognition. I think the distinction is between someone who did not know the accused prior to the incident and someone who did. We can theoretically encounter, and may well encounter in this case, those points where the two points come close to intersecting, and that is with a witness who knew the accused from before the incident but only on the basis of a small number of contacts. In that case, the Defence, for example, may choose to attack the witness's recognition, and assert that in fact the witness's prior exposure to the accused did not give him a sufficient basis for recognising the accused at the time of the incident. In that case, the witness's selection of the accused from amongst a photo array demonstrates his ability to recognise the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Of course, the problem there is very obvious and you are well aware of it, that he may be looking at the photo array and identifying, not based on his view of the accused at Omarska, say, but based on prior knowledge. Everyone understands that and there is no problem about it. It is a factor that affects weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. I do not want to confuse the two concepts, of course. That is why I think it is useful to separate the two issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Mr. Wladimiroff, do you intend or do you want to offer testimony of Professor Wagenaar?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. If it will be possible to hear him at half past five or between 4.00 and half past five.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Between 4.00 and 5.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Between 4.00 and half past 4, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Between 4.00 and 4.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, is there an objection to hearing from Professor Wagenaar?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. As the Court may have noticed in the written response, it is the Prosecution's position that the Defence has raised an issue of the admissibility of the photospread. Our position is that there is no precondition or test which the Prosecution in any jurisdiction is required to meet in order to introduce such evidence. To the extent that weighing factor may exist in some jurisdictions, it largely goes to the question of what is going to be in front of the jury. In any event, it is never reduced to the contention that a specific experimental procedure needs to be conducted before the Prosecution can introduce evidence which is clearly probative. The Defence is obviously free after the admission of such evidence, the introduction of such evidence, to attack the weight to which the court will give the evidence, but that is a whole different matter from the admissibility. The fact that Dr. Wagenaar is involved in this instance is simply because the Prosecution attempted, in good faith, to resolve this issue with the Defence prior to trial. We knew at the time, as we know now, that no such test is required, nor does the photo line-up which is very exacting need such a test to be admissible, but in discussions with the Defence, they advised that we could eliminate this as a trial issue if we submitted to Dr. Wagenaar, about whom we both knew, and he approved it. Because we had confidence in the line-up and because we wanted to resolve this before trial we presented it. He did approve it. That is the status of this matter. If we want to take a step back, we are simply back where we were before, which is that there is no prerequisite for the admissibility of this. The Defence in its own case can call appropriate witnesses to attack the Prosecution evidence, but this evidence should simply be heard and the Defence motion is misplaced. In any event, if any test or any sort of test was required, that test was conducted by Dr. Wagenaar and the test was approved.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have anything to add on that point before you go directly on to your argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is not clear to me, to be frank, if the Prosecution is saying, yes, we do object. As a matter of fact, they only made comments. If I may comment on these issues too. We did discuss with the Prosecution something different, that is a video line-up. That is what we discussed last year. It has been confirmed in the letter of October 28th and I wrote to the Prosecution that Mr. Tadic is inclined to co-operate when the Prosecutor's office will produce a video tape for the purposes of confrontation and possible recognition by witnesses, if the Prosecution is able to meet with the following conditions and, indeed, there Professor Wagenaar appears. That letter ended: Once a list of all requirements for the production of the video tape is completed, the Defence will consult its own experts and may formulate additional conditions before it will take its final decision whether it grants to co-operate or not. That is exactly what we did discuss.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So what you are saying is there really was no agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, certainly not. At the very beginning of this year we met again with the Prosecution about identification and we told them that we are considering a video tape ourselves. Then they told us they had this photospread and that is all we knew. It was not discussed in terms of, so what is this photospread about? Can we have a look? How was it done and has it been checked by Professor Wagenaar? Nothing of that kind. We just got information that there was a photospread. As a matter of fact, the first time we saw this photospread was on June 7th. So I think there has been some misunderstanding here. We have discussed extensively the issue of a video line-up but not of a photo line up. The second issue then is the evidence to be given by Professor Wagenaar today I think is very helpful for your Court to understand what is the meaning of this test, since he has tested the test. You have read this letter and you will have noticed that his comments are on the assumption that, for example, the ethnic component is not a problem. But, as a matter of fact, Dr. Wagenaar only responded to the question that was put to him. He did not answer to any other question that might arise after reading the letter which had been raised by the Defence and, therefore, I made this objection, at least I made this submission last week. We feel that it would be very helpful for the Court to understand what has been done with this test, what is this meaning of this test, what are the problems here, and what does research learn about the pitfalls in these kinds of things. We would like to have Professor Wagenaar to explain to you what are the problems here, so you can appreciate the arguments of the Defence as well as those of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do agree that it would be helpful. The question is whether it is helpful now. That is the question. (The Judges conferred).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: By a majority of the Chamber we have determined not to hear Dr. Wagenaar at this time. Let me explain why. You are very correct that his testimony will be very helpful to us because he will be talking about this process, but I am sure you yourself have tried many, many a case where statistics particularly, that is what I recall, have been involved. I have heard, for example, from witnesses from one side about all of these statistics and what is the model and what is a standard statistical deviation, etc., and one side takes the position that X is the standard statistical deviation. Then I hear from the other side. I have never heard of Defence interceding I suppose before the moving party offers the evidence with their expert witness to tell the Court, and to tell the Prosecution or the moving party if it is a civil case, that is this is improper. This is why we have and we allow experts to be excluded from the Rule, so that experts on each side can remain in the courtroom and hear testimony about which they may later comment and give at the appropriate time their testimony with respect to that evidence. The other concern I suppose that does not really fit here, is that you do not have a jury. The problem so often with a jury, as we well know, those of us who come from systems where there is a jury, is that you just cannot -- I almost said you cannot unscramble the eggs, I do not mean that. I mean it is difficult to unscramble the eggs, because what you do in a jury situation is you allow sometimes evidence to come in and then you instruct the jury to disregard that evidence. Of course, we all know, particularly as lawyers, that it is sometimes difficult for them to disregard the evidence, although I do believe juries do a good job. You do not have that problem here. We Judges intentionally and specifically in drafting the Rules of Evidence provide for the opportunity in 89(D) I think it is, 89(D), that a Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. The intent behind that is that obviously this is probative evidence, but it may turn out that notwithstanding it being probative, we may be so convinced after we hear at the appropriate time from other expert witnesses that this is just totally improper, we may make the determination that we should exclude it, but we do that in an orderly process. I would not want to set the precedent of interrupting a trial of a criminal case so that one party can judge the appropriateness of the opposing party proceeding in a certain way. The way it is typically done, as I say, is to have your expert witness here, listen to what has happened and then, if you wish, at the appropriate time challenge it with that expert testimony, but not to give it early on. Also, although it is helpful to us when it comes early on, it is difficult for us to put it in the proper frame. So that we hear from him, and we hear very scholarly, important pronouncements, but until you are able to actually put it in context, the real value is not there. The other matter is that you have submitted to us with your submission a submission from Dr. Wagenaar. We have now from the Prosecutor something from Dr. Wagenaar. We have before us enough at this point from Dr. Wagenaar. Of course, you are free, should you choose, to challenge this evidence in any way, and that may include by calling an expert witness, which is typically the way that it is done, and then challenge the whole procedure and say it is not scientifically probative. So, I will deny that request but we may proceed with argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to an aspect that struck, at least, the Defence. In a proper conduct of proceedings, once the Judge has made his decision or the court has made its decision, it is very likely that the court will be consistent in any further step of the proceedings not to reconsider its decision. It will keep on the same track. That is what we feel. Just as a blanket example, your court ruled that a dock identification is appropriate in this case and so far we have no reason to believe that you will change your rulings on that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If there has been an appropriate foundation laid, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely. We have heard you saying that and we have appreciated that, so that is your ruling. The next time again you will rule in conformity with that ruling. What we feel here is that if we are going to argue today the value of any evidence to be given on the basis of that test, you might give a ruling on that and maybe later on in our case in-chief you will hear evidence from Professor Wagenaar and we fear that it will be quite difficult for you to reverse what you have decided today. So we rather prefer you to understand what is the real meaning of this evidence if it is put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There will be no dock identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, but I give it just as an example. Once you have decided for a dock identification, every new witnesses you will accept, if he recognised Tadic in court on the basis of a brief knowledge of Tadic, we may object but you will rule consistently.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not believe that if we hear Dr. Wagenaar at the appropriate time, and Dr. Wagenaar in the role of an expert will testify about the procedure and testify that the procedure utilized by the Prosecution is invalid and should not be given and does not have probative value because it was not conducted in accordance with accepted scientific procedures, if that were to be his testimony and we accept it, and we accept it, then out goes that evidence, out goes that evidence, Mr. Wladimiroff. I assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But what, your Honour, if someone is recognised here in court in a dock ID, because he also recognised him on the basis of photographs that have been shown to the witness before he identifies, and what implications of that identification will there be? Then you have given judicial notice that there was an identification and you cannot reverse that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, well, I think this, I think the proper way to handle it is what we have done in the past, and that is we have allowed dock identification if a proper foundation has been laid. It seems to me that what you are asserting now is that the foundation would be an identification through a photospread which may be invalidated by Dr. Wagenaar's testimony as a witness of the Defence. If that is the only foundation, then out goes the dock identification as well. It is very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is very assuring.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, for sure, because we have been very clear to say it is a matter of foundation. The witnesses we have heard from, witnesses who have, you know, gone to school with Mr. Tadic or had other contacts, and being satisfied that there was a sufficient foundation we allow the dock identification. It is not that we are allowing dock identification in principle because, of course, you are correct; you look across and you see a gentleman between two officers and, you know, you do not have to be a rocket scientist to understand that it is either one of these officers or it is Mr. Tadic. So I accept that and I understand your reason for objecting, but we feel compelled to overrule the objection, having found a proper foundation. If the only foundation is something that is demonstrated to us to be improper, then what is based on that foundation goes out of the window as well, I assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understand the position of the court. I think, your Honour, I wanted to confer with the Defence whether it will be in technical terms wise to argue then what I wanted to argue. I wanted to consider the possibility of dealing with the issue in our case in-chief then, because I think it should be connected with the evidence of Dr. Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: A 15 minute recess, is that enough time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, would you like to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have decided not to pursue the matter at this moment and to keep our submission pending until we will present our case in-chief because we feel we would rather argue the matter with the evidence of Dr. Wagenaar. Therefore, we ask you to keep the matter pending until that date.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. We have now the submission that you gave us for Dr. Wagenaar and the Prosecution has given us a submission too, but you do not want to stand on your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We want that submission pending.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, we will take it ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Under advisement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- we will just keep it under advisement and rule on it after we have had the benefit of whatever other evidence, either evidence you wish to offer, or testimony, or whatever else you wish to offer. Mr. Tieger? I said you could release your witnesses, so now what do we do? Do you have a witness available we could finish with by 5.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour, we do not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. A couple of matters. The Defence has filed a motion on hearsay just today, I gather, and the Prosecution needs to respond to that within 14 days from today. What we would like to do is to set a hearing on that because you have requested a hearing, I understand, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will have a hearing on that the first day that we are in session again which will be Tuesday, July 16th. So, the Prosecutor is to file a response within 14 calendar days. We will hear this on July 16th at 10 a.m. Are there other matters that counsel would like to bring to the attention of the court at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, just a practical matter. I have not checked with my box at this moment but I take it that your decision of 7th May will be in that box?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be by the time you get down stairs if it is not already. Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, may I address a few remarks to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You recall the other day I congratulated you on using 20 minutes for a witness and I think you estimated that that witness would take to two to three hours I think it was. I appreciate that, although I understand that you need to present your case in-chief efficiently. However, we want it to be done expeditiously as well. So I want just to give you a kind of summary of what I have done, what has been done actually by Miss Featherstone, regarding the witnesses we have heard by count and the number that are left to be heard. For count 1 we have heard, that is for witnesses you have listed who would testify as to count 1 only, we have heard 11 witnesses and we have 29 left to be heard. For counts 5 through 11 we have heard one and we have 12 left to be heard. For counts 12 to 14 we have two left to be heard. For counts 15 to 17 we have three left to be heard. For counts 18 to 20 we have one left to be heard. For counts 21 to 23 we have two left to be heard. For counts 24 through 28 we have heard three witnesses and we have one left to be heard. For counts 29 through 34 we have heard none and we have six to be heard. So while we are in recess because of the need of the other Trial Chamber to have access to the only courtroom that we have, I would encourage you to take a look at the evidence that you intend to offer, take a look at the witnesses you intend to offer as to the counts, particularly count one -- I understand that a multiplicity of acts are charged and it is persecution in count 1, but you have 29 witnesses left to be heard on that and we have already heard -- take a look to see, see what you can do to pare it down, if you can, to what you consider to be absolutely necessary to sustain your burden. I do not mean to be heavy-handed. I know I have asked more than once or twice for the Prosecutor to consider the evidence that you have and perhaps handling it more expeditiously if it is possible. I have heard you say that this is the first case that is being tried and that you have concerns about it, but I will ask that perhaps since you have more than one counsel sometimes it might be nice -- I am not suggesting that you do not --to confer with each other to make sure that you do not have too much overlap. So, having heard that, do you have any remarks or would you do that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have of course addressed this on numerous occasions among ourselves in an endeavour to pare down the list of witnesses. I think that perhaps can be illustrated by the fact there are two lists: one which is the list we are calling and the other of those witnesses that could be called but they are ones we have sacrificed, in a sense, in an effort to reduce the number. We will, of course, take up what your Honour says and re-examine the position to see whether or not we can reduce the number of witnesses. We do this on an ongoing basis in any event. We will also look at the prospect of keeping the evidence down to its absolute minimum, so that the length of time witnesses take is kept to a minimum. In some instances, your Honours, we certainly take the view that this evidence is very important, very important for the Prosecution case. It is often very difficult when you have a witness that has one central point which is very important and there are other pieces of evidence which are also relevant, it is often difficult, you cannot disband that witness because the witness is important for that point, but it is often difficult to contain the witness to that specific point and simply dismiss at the end of that piece of evidence. This is a problem which obviously occurs from time to time. We are conscious, your Honours, of the amount of time it takes. We are conscious of the number of witnesses. Your Honours, although it is not the biggest case we have presented before this Tribunal, it is very unusual in the sense that most jurisdictions do not normally encounter a case with multiple murders, a multiple variety of types of offences, rapes and serious assaults, which occurred in this case. It is a massive case and massive cases call for a massive amount of evidence to be called. My experience in other jurisdictions is that cases just with 20 murders, I know of one that ran for something like eight months. This is a case which is even bigger than that. So we are trying, your Honours, to keep it down but it is not easy. We are trying to be as economical with the Court time as possible, but we will try even harder.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We looked at one option I guess that you had proposed, and that is additional hours, longer hours, and perhaps hearing the case on Monday. We had indicated that we could not because again we have one courtroom. The other Chamber needs this courtroom on Monday. We need this courtroom on Monday. We have conducted a number of matters in this courtroom while hearing the Tadic case. We now hear testimony I guess of about five and a half hours a day, and the only way for us to extend the hours would be to have two teams of interpreters and we already have six or seven. That would mean that we would have to double that number which would be absolutely astronomical. So there is not too much we can do as Judges to extend it. I am asking you once again to take a look, since we will have this two-week period, take a look to see what can be done. We are patient. Our job as Judges is to sit here and listen, but it is also our job in a sense to direct the parties and to direct them to act in an expeditious and appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, can I ask you in relation to this motion on hearsay, you have heard our President say to the Prosecution that they have 14 days with which to respond. I may be misunderstanding the relief you seek, but it seems to me that we could grant the relief you seek and change nothing, because the first item of relief is “refuse to hear hearsay evidence”, in effect, and then, secondly, however, “discretion to hear it if it considers its probative value substantially outweighs its prejudicial effect”, which is, word for word, Rule 89(D). So I do not see that you change anything by getting the relief that you seek. I just wonder whether it is going to be easy for the Prosecution to respond when your relief is in this form. All I can say is, would you give that some consideration? It may be I misunderstood your application.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am pleased to do so, your Honour. The Defence takes it that you are not reading our motion in a very cynical way, but simply do not understand what we are heading for. At least, what want is to open the possibility to have the criteria to argue when this balance has to be done, because now on the basis of Rule 89(D) we are not in a position to argue that hearsay is on that balance. In general, each evidence has to be balanced and you accept hearsay evidence, as we appreciate so far. We rather prefer that it should not be accepted unless there are good arguments and reason to do so, and then on the balance of 89(D) you may accept it. So there is a step in between that gives room to us to argue that you should not, because your initial position is not to accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think the very fact that you have said what you have said clarifies the situation as far as I am concerned and may also be of some help to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I can, if I may just add to that. I am looking back over the evidence, I have not reviewed it, but I do remember really only one, perhaps two, objections that have been made on hearsay by the Defence. One had to do with Mrs. Klipic, I believe who testified, and she was offering testimony about a death. The testimony was that she heard from someone who saw something occur at a camp, and I am not even sure that that person saw something but may have been told by someone else about that. As I recall, the objection was sustained as to anything other than the fact of death, other than the fact that (and you can go back and see) the person was dead, but anything else we did not want to hear. The reason for the ruling really did not relate to hearsay so much, but the fact that it is no longer probative. Probative means that it is supportive of the facts that are asserted. If it is not, then it is not coming in, whether it is hearsay or whether it is some other word that we put. That was one. There was another objection I think that Mr. Kay made because it did involve an identity of Mr. Tadic. I do not recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It was the case with the church, you will remember.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That is when we got into the exception as an excited, well, we spoke of it as an excited utterance. Again this all comes from different systems, but the reason why excited utterance is hearsay but is admissible as an exception is that it has probative value, some trustworthiness, because it is assumed that people in that excited manner will not fabricate and that we allow to come in. We do have some time over the recess. You may want to take a look at the transcript and see what you have been dissatisfied with in terms of rulings on the basis of -- I do not want to specify the dissatisfaction, I would limit it to one point, and that has to do with evidence coming in that you would consider not probative, not probative because it is hearsay. If you will do that, then perhaps you can point us to what it is you are talking about, because Judge Stephen is right, as a general matter hearsay evidence is admissible. This is an International Tribunal, three Judges, and believe me it was thoroughly debated as to whether or not hearsay. If I had my druthers the case -- there we go, "druthers", that America saying -- might happen differently because of what I am accustomed to and I am accustomed to hearsay evidence not coming in. That is not true in civil systems and that is certainly not true in an International Tribunal where you have three Judges. So I do not want to convince you. I do not know that I can convince you and if you choose to offer evidence I am going to have to convince the other side. But we are listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Once again, also in this matter we filed a motion not only reviewing what has been decided so far on those two occasions, but also knowing what may come up with future witnesses. We feel that we should discuss the matter now in order to give structure if you are going to rule next time again.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Stephen is much quicker than I am and I have not looked at it, but again hearsay evidence in war crimes -- we will look at it. We will look at it. If you are not talking about, if it is not a criticism, a direct criticism of what has happened in the past, but more of a suggestion that we approach matters differently in the future, or certainly in the future, that is fine. But if it is something else, then you need to look at the transcript. I am pretty confident of what we have done thus far and that is, yes, when there is an objection that has been made I think that what has come in in the very few cases where there has been an objection does have probative value. Other hearsay evidence has come in a lot on the policy without objection, but that is background information. So handle it the way you want. Judge Stephen's point was that we certainly do not want the Prosecutor giving us a response saying, well, the Rules say that we can do this. If that is true, then we have not really accomplished too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It might be difficult, but we will try to explain that to you after the recess.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Very good. Then we will adjourn until, unfortunately, until July 16th at 10 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: (The court adjourned for a short time)
